snip.t: With acute renal infection, leukocytosis and neutrophilia are noted on the complete blood count (CBC); an elevated serum erythrocyte sedimentation rate, procalcitonin level, and C-reactive protein are common.
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) in normal pregnancy is typically:
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): General marker of inflammation. — Usually normal or mildly elevated in PCP.
Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and C-reactive Protein (CRP): These markers of inflammation may be elevated in inflammatory myopathies.

Elevations of the C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and procalcitonin can be seen in both bacterial and viral meningitis and should not be used to routinely determine which patients should receive antimicrobials.

qs.q: A 25-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation has blood tests showing an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and a raised white cell count in the absence of infection. Why is the ESR considered unreliable in this patient?
o: Hemodilution falsely lowers the sedimentation rate regardless of inflammation
Progesterone actively suppresses the sedimentation reflex in erythrocytes
Increased maternal renal clearance removes acute phase reactants
Normal physiological changes of pregnancy independently elevate the ESR
qs.e: White cell count and ESR rise during normal pregnancy, rendering the ESR unreliable for diagnosing inflammatory conditions. Dilutional anaemia and altered plasma proteins contribute to this laboratory shift.
qs.s: Physiological Changes of Pregnancy by System: MCQs

qs.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with an intensely tender anterior neck mass, low-grade fever, and palpitations following an upper respiratory tract infection. Laboratory evaluation reveals a suppressed TSH and a markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: De Quervain subacute granulomatous thyroiditis typically follows viral infections, presenting with neck pain and an elevated ESR. Hashimoto thyroiditis presents as a painless goiter with hypothyroidism rather than a painful tender gland with thyrotoxicosis.
qs.s: Year 3: Endocrine and Metabolic Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) alongside hyperlipidemia. Which laboratory alteration contributes directly to the elevated ESR in this clinical setting?
qs.e: In nephrotic syndrome, the liver increases protein synthesis including lipoproteins and fibrinogen, where the increased serum fibrinogen drives up the ESR. Platelet count changes do not primarily dictate the ESR elevation here.

qs.q: During the evaluation of a pediatric patient with pyrexia of unknown origin, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) greater than 100 mm is strongly associated with which of the following conditions?
qs.e: An ESR greater than 100 mm indicates severe inflammation pointing towards TB, malignancy, autoimmune conditions, or Kawasaki disease. Mild infections typically present with lower elevation.

qs.q: The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) in normal pregnancy is typically
o: Decreased due to reduced erythrocyte aggregation
Markedly elevated due to increased fibrinogen
Low in the first and second trimesters, rising in the third
qs.e: Pregnancy increases plasma fibrinogen and other acute phase proteins, promoting red cell rouleaux and raising ESR.

ai.title: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate measures the distance red blood cells fall in anticoagulated whole blood over one hour. It serves as an indirect marker of systemic inflammation driven by asymmetric plasma proteins like fibrinogen. It is highly sensitive but non-specific.

sections.p: ESR is an indirect measure of the acute-phase response. Normally, negative surface charges (zeta potential) keep erythrocytes apart. In inflammatory states, asymmetric acute-phase proteins (chiefly fibrinogen and immunoglobulins) neutralize these charges, promoting stacking into rouleaux that fall faster through plasma.
b: Reference range for men: age divided by 2 in mm/hour
Reference range for women: (age plus 10) divided by 2 in mm/hour
Measured in anticoagulated blood left vertical for 60 minutes
Westergren method is the gold standard clinical reference

sections.p: Clinicians interpret the magnitude of ESR elevation to narrow down broad diagnostic categories.
b: Normal to mildly elevated (below 50 mm/hour): non-specific, seen in localized infection, obesity, or advanced age
Moderately elevated (50 to 99 mm/hour): common in systemic infections, active autoimmune diseases, and localized malignancies
Markedly elevated (100 mm/hour or more): strongly indicates tuberculosis, occult deep-seated bacterial infection, multiple myeloma, or systemic vasculitis

sections.p: In resource-limited and tropical settings, infectious and clonal hematologic etiologies must be considered before primary autoimmune diseases.
b: Chronic infections: pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis, visceral leishmaniasis, infective endocarditis, and chronic osteomyelitis
HIV-associated conditions: advanced HIV infection itself or concurrent opportunistic infections (though typically normal or mildly elevated in PCP)
Malignancies: multiple myeloma, lymphoma, and metastatic solid tumors (e.g., renal cell carcinoma)
Rheumatologic and vasculitic disease: giant cell arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, systemic lupus erythematosus, and rheumatoid arthritis
Acute rheumatic fever: major laboratory criteria when presenting with carditis, arthritis, or chorea
Physiologic states: pregnancy (typically elevated) and advanced age

sections.p: ESR is a laboratory test rather than a clinical entity; patients present with the underlying condition driving the inflammation.
b: Prolonged fever, drenching night sweats, and profound weight loss (tuberculosis, lymphoma)
Bone pain and pathological fractures in elderly patients (multiple myeloma)
New-onset unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, or visual disturbances in patients over 50 (giant cell arteritis)
Migratory large-joint polyarthritis with chorea or carditis (acute rheumatic fever)
Severe morning joint stiffness persisting over 30 minutes (rheumatoid arthritis)

t.a: Full blood count with peripheral film
t.b: Rules out severe anemia which falsely elevates ESR; detects rouleaux, leukocytosis, or leukemic blasts.
Determines acute versus chronic inflammation; CRP rises and normalizes faster than ESR.
Detects monoclonal paraprotein bands driving extreme rouleaux formation in multiple myeloma.
Identifies Mycobacterium tuberculosis in patients with unexplained markedy high ESR and cough.
Identifies proteinuria or Bence-Jones protein; rules out nephrotic syndrome or chronic kidney disease elevating ESR.
Identifies endovascular or occult bacteremia prior to starting empiric antimicrobials.

sections.p: An isolated abnormal ESR never causes direct tissue injury, but extreme elevations or specific clinical contexts require emergency action to prevent death or permanent disability.
b: Sudden vision loss with high ESR: urgent temporal arteritis treatment needed to protect sight
ESR of 100 mm/hour or more with back pain: urgent evaluation for tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott disease) or myeloma spinal cord compression
High ESR with fever and murmur: requires urgent echocardiogram and blood cultures for infective endocarditis

sections.p: Management focuses entirely on identifying and treating the underlying disease. Never treat an isolated elevated ESR with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or steroids without an established etiology.
b: Anti-tuberculous therapy: initiated when diagnostic criteria for active tuberculosis are met
Systemic corticosteroids: initiated promptly if giant cell arteritis is suspected, avoiding delay for biopsy to prevent irreversible blindness
Targeted antimicrobials: guided by blood cultures for osteomyelitis or infective endocarditis
Supportive hydration: in multiple myeloma to reduce renal light-chain precipitation and manage hypercalcemia
Antiretroviral therapy: instituted appropriately for underlying HIV infection once acute opportunists are stabilized

sections.p: ESR changes slowly because fibrinogen has a biological half-life of several days to weeks.
b: Do not repeat ESR daily or within 48 hours; it reflects past, not immediate, inflammation
Use CRP for monitoring rapid responses to treatment in acute bacterial infections
Recheck ESR every 2 to 4 weeks when monitoring chronic conditions like giant cell arteritis or osteomyelitis
Falling ESR alongside clinical improvement confirms effective suppression of the primary driver

sections.p: Clinicians frequently confuse the clinical roles and performance characteristics of acute-phase reactants.
b: C-reactive protein (CRP): CRP responds within 6 hours and clears rapidly; ESR rises over 24 to 48 hours and persists for weeks
Procalcitonin: specific for invasive bacterial infection; ESR and CRP can be elevated in both bacterial and viral infections
Plasma viscosity: independent of red cell factors and shapes; useful when severe anemia or hemoglobinopathies distort ESR

sections.p: Both hematologic anomalies and physical factors can create falsely high or falsely low values.
b: Severe anemia falsely raises ESR by decreasing internal resistance to settling erythrocytes
Polycythemia falsely lowers ESR because high hematocrit impedes downward cell movement
Sickle cell anemia and spherocytosis falsely lower ESR because abnormal cell shapes prevent rouleaux formation
Pregnancy is typically associated with elevated ESR due to physiological rise in fibrinogen
Tilted sedimentation tubes or warm ambient room temperatures falsely accelerate erythrocyte settling
Normal or mildly elevated in PCP despite significant pulmonary disease

faq.q: Can ESR distinguish between bacterial and viral meningitis?
faq.a: No. Elevations of CRP, ESR, and procalcitonin can occur in both and must not be used alone to direct antimicrobial decisions.

faq.q: Why is ESR almost zero in sickle cell anemia?
faq.a: Sickled erythrocytes are mechanically rigid and cannot physically stack into rouleaux, preventing accelerated sedimentation even during severe systemic inflammation.

faq.q: How does extreme anemia affect the interpretation of ESR?
faq.a: Anemia reduces the crowded cell effect in the tube, allowing cells to fall faster and producing a falsely high ESR.

exam: A 72-year-old with headache has an ESR of 98 mm/hour; what is your immediate action? — Initiate high-dose systemic corticosteroids immediately before scheduling a temporal artery biopsy to prevent ischemic optic neuropathy and permanent blindness.

Why does a patient with high-grade fever and sickle cell disease have an ESR of 2 mm/hour? — Sickled erythrocytes cannot form rouleaux due to their altered membrane shape and rigidity, causing a falsely low ESR despite marked inflammation.

Why prefer CRP over ESR when monitoring antibiotic response in acute bacterial osteomyelitis? — CRP has a much shorter half-life and normalizes within days of successful therapy, whereas ESR remains elevated for weeks after inflammation resolves.

A patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis has severe microcytic anemia and an ESR of 115 mm/hour; how do you interpret this? — The marked elevation may be partly artifactual due to reduced hematocrit, although tuberculosis itself is a classic cause of ESR exceeding 100 mm/hour.

Why is ESR physiologically elevated in a healthy third-trimester pregnant woman? — Pregnancy induces a physiological rise in plasma fibrinogen, which neutralizes the erythrocyte negative surface charge and accelerates rouleaux formation.

In a patient with suspected Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, what do you expect the ESR to show? — The ESR is typically normal or only mildly elevated in PCP, unlike the marked elevations seen in bacterial pneumonia or tuberculosis.

What non-inflammatory technical errors can falsely increase the Westergren ESR? — Tilting the Westergren tube away from vertical, high ambient laboratory temperature, and prolonged duration before reading the tube.
